name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_3D_REPRESENTATION_MCQ_Q01 - Interpretation of dashed wedge in three-dimensional structure

questiontext.text:
The three-dimensional structure of a methane molecule is represented using the wedge-and-dash convention shown in the diagram below:

What spatial orientation does Bond X represent according to standard stereochemical conventions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Diagram Interpretation
The diagram illustrates the three-dimensional representation of a tetrahedral methane (\(\mathrm{CH}_4\)) molecule drawn using standard wedge-and-dash conventions. In this representation:

  • Normal solid lines denote covalent bonds lying entirely within the plane of the paper.
  • A solid wedge indicates a bond pointing forward, projecting out of the plane towards the observer.
  • Bond X is drawn as a series of parallel lines increasing in breadth (a dashed wedge).

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Conventions
According to IUPAC stereochemical conventions for projecting three-dimensional structures onto a two-dimensional sheet of paper:

  • The normal line (\(-\)) represents a bond lying in the plane of the paper.
  • The solid wedge represents a bond projecting out of the plane of paper, directed towards the observer.
  • The dashed wedge represents a bond projecting out of the plane of paper, directed away from the observer.

Step 3: Evaluation of Bond X
Bond X is depicted as a dashed wedge originating from the central carbon atom. Therefore, it unambiguously denotes a bond projecting away from the observer behind the plane of the paper.

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
The dashed wedge specifically denotes the bond directed away from the observer behind the plane of the paper. Hence, the correct statement is that it represents a bond projecting out of the plane of the paper and away from the observer.

answer.text: A bond projecting out of the plane of the paper and away from the observer
A bond projecting out of the plane of the paper and towards the observer
A bond lying entirely within the plane of the paper
A delocalised \(\pi\)-bond shared equally among the hydrogen atoms

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_HYPERCONJUGATION_ORBITAL_MCQ_Q02 - Orbital interaction in ethyl carbocation stabilization

questiontext.text:
The diagram below depicts the orbital interaction responsible for the stabilization of the ethyl cation (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\overset{+}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_2\)):

Which electronic displacement effect and specific orbital overlap are illustrated in this diagram?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Diagram Interpretation
The orbital schematic shows:

  • An alkyl methyl carbon possessing a \(\mathrm{C}(sp^3)-\mathrm{H}(1s)\) \(\sigma\)-bond.
  • An adjacent positively charged carbocationic carbon possessing an empty unhybridised \(2p\) orbital perpendicular to the plane of bonding.
  • A sideways overlap showing electron density delocalising from the filled \(\sigma_{\mathrm{C-H}}\) orbital into the vacant \(2p\) orbital.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Electronic Displacement Effects
Hyperconjugation is a permanent stabilising interaction that involves the delocalisation of \(\sigma\)-electrons belonging to a \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond of an alkyl group directly attached to an atom with an unshared or empty \(p\) orbital (or to an unsaturated system). This overlap disperses the positive charge over adjacent atoms, thereby enhancing the stability of the cation.

Step 3: Elimination of Alternative Effects
- The inductive effect operates strictly through \(\sigma\)-bonds via electronegativity differences without involving empty \(p\) orbitals or orbital overlap.
- The electromeric effect is a temporary complete shift of \(\pi\)-electrons in multiple bonds demanded by an attacking reagent.
- The resonance effect involves the interaction of two \(\pi\)-bonds or a \(\pi\)-bond and a non-bonding lone pair, not \(\sigma_{\mathrm{C-H}}\) bonds.

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
The interaction represents hyperconjugation via the overlap of the \(\sigma_{\mathrm{C-H}}\) orbital with the adjacent vacant \(2p\) orbital of the positively charged carbon atom.

answer.text: Hyperconjugation involving delocalisation of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{C-H}}\) electrons into the empty \(2p\) orbital of the carbocation
Positive resonance effect (\(+R\)) involving lateral overlap between two parallel \(2p\) orbitals
Inductive effect (\(+I\)) involving electron displacement through the \(\mathrm{C-C}\) \(\sigma\)-bond without orbital overlap
Electromeric effect (\(+E\)) involving temporary transfer of \(\pi\)-electrons to the carbocation centre

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_TLC_CHROMATOGRAPHY_MCQ_Q03 - Determination of Rf value from thin layer chromatogram

questiontext.text:
A thin layer chromatography (TLC) plate coated with silica gel was developed in a suitable organic solvent. The developed chromatogram with experimental measurements is shown below:

What is the retardation factor (\(R_f\) value) of the compound?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the provided developed chromatogram:

  • Distance moved by the substance spot from the base line, \(x = 3.2\text{ cm}\).
  • Distance moved by the solvent front from the base line, \(y = 8.0\text{ cm}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The retardation factor (\(R_f\)) in chromatography is defined as: \[ R_f = \frac{\text{Distance moved by the substance from base line } (x)}{\text{Distance moved by the solvent from base line } (y)} \]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the measured values into the expression: \[ R_f = \frac{3.2\text{ cm}}{8.0\text{ cm}} = \frac{32}{80} = \frac{4}{10} = 0.40 \]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The \(R_f\) value must be dimensionless and lie strictly in the range \(0 \le R_f \le 1\). The calculated value \(0.40\) is consistent with the physical position of the spot located below the midpoint of the solvent travel path. Thus, the retardation factor is \(0.40\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_CARBANION_STRUCTURE_MCQ_Q04 - Geometry and hybridisation state of methyl carbanion

questiontext.text:
The electronic structure and spatial geometry of a carbon-containing reactive intermediate are shown below:

Which intermediate, carbon hybridisation state, and molecular geometry are represented in this figure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Diagram Interpretation
The diagram illustrates a trivalent carbon intermediate bearing a negative charge and an unshared non-bonding electron pair housed inside a directed hybrid orbital. Three \(\mathrm{C-H}\) single bonds project downward in a non-planar arrangement.

Step 2: Fundamental Principles of Reactive Intermediates
- A heterolytic cleavage in which the carbon atom retains the shared electron pair forms a carbanion (\(\mathrm{R}_3\mathrm{C}^-\)).
- In a simple alkyl carbanion such as the methyl carbanion (\(:\overset{-}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3\)), the central carbon has a total of 8 valence electrons (6 bonding electrons forming three \(\mathrm{C-H}\) \(\sigma\)-bonds and 2 non-bonding electrons forming a lone pair).
- The central carbon is \(sp^3\) hybridised, with three hybrid orbitals forming \(\sigma\)-bonds and the fourth hybrid orbital accommodating the lone pair.
- Due to lone pair–bond pair repulsions, the three \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds are pushed downwards away from the orbital holding the lone pair, giving a distorted tetrahedral (pyramidal) shape, isoelectronic with ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)).

Step 3: Contrast with Other Intermediates
- A methyl carbocation (\(\overset{+}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3\)) has only six valence electrons, is \(sp^2\) hybridised, and possesses a trigonal planar geometry with an empty unhybridised \(2p\) orbital.
- A carbon free radical (\(\dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3\)) is neutral and contains seven valence electrons with a single unpaired electron.

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
The species depicted is a methyl carbanion with an \(sp^3\) hybridised carbon and a pyramidal (distorted tetrahedral) geometry.

answer.text: Methyl carbanion; \(sp^3\) hybridised carbon; distorted tetrahedral (pyramidal) geometry
Methyl carbocation; \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon; trigonal planar geometry
Methyl free radical; \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon; planar geometry
Methyl carbanion; \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon; trigonal planar geometry

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_LIEBIG_COMBUSTION_MCQ_Q05 - Reagents and functions in carbon and hydrogen quantitative estimation apparatus

questiontext.text:
The schematic diagram below illustrates the apparatus used in Liebig's combustion method for the simultaneous quantitative estimation of carbon and hydrogen present in an organic compound:

Which chemical reagents are contained in Tube 1 and Tube 2 respectively, and what are their specific analytical absorption functions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram illustrates the Liebig combustion train containing:

  • A combustion tube where an organic compound undergoes complete oxidation with dry \(\mathrm{O}_2\) in the presence of hot copper(II) oxide (\(\mathrm{CuO}\)).
  • Carbon is oxidised to \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and hydrogen is oxidised to \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).
  • Two absorption U-tubes connected in sequence: Tube 1 followed by Tube 2.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Chemical Reactions
1. The gaseous combustion products passing out of the furnace contain steam (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)), carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\)), and unreacted \(\mathrm{O}_2\).
2. Water vapour must be removed first before carbon dioxide because alkaline solutions that absorb \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) also absorb water vapour.
3. Anhydrous calcium chloride (\(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\)) is a neutral hygroscopic desiccant that selectively absorbs water vapour without reacting with acidic \(\mathrm{CO}_2\). Hence, Tube 1 contains anhydrous \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\).
4. The dry gas stream containing \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) then enters Tube 2, which contains a concentrated solution of potassium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{KOH}\)). \(\mathrm{KOH}\) selectively absorbs acidic \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) according to the neutralization reaction: \[ 2\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{CO}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{CO}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \]

Step 3: Verification of Sequence
- If Tube 1 contained \(\mathrm{KOH}\), it would absorb both \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) simultaneously, making independent estimation of hydrogen and carbon impossible.
- Therefore, Tube 1 must contain anhydrous \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) (to absorb \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) and Tube 2 must contain concentrated \(\mathrm{KOH}\) solution (to absorb \(\mathrm{CO}_2\)).

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
Tube 1 contains anhydrous \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) to absorb \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), and Tube 2 contains concentrated \(\mathrm{KOH}\) solution to absorb \(\mathrm{CO}_2\).

answer.text: Tube 1 contains anhydrous \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) to absorb \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\); Tube 2 contains concentrated \(\mathrm{KOH}\) solution to absorb \(\mathrm{CO}_2\)
Tube 1 contains concentrated \(\mathrm{KOH}\) solution to absorb \(\mathrm{CO}_2\); Tube 2 contains anhydrous \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) to absorb \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)
Tube 1 contains anhydrous \(\mathrm{CuSO}_4\) to absorb \(\mathrm{CO}_2\); Tube 2 contains soda lime to absorb \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)
Tube 1 contains concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to absorb \(\mathrm{CO}_2\); Tube 2 contains solid \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) to absorb \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_DUMAS_NITROMETER_MCQ_Q06 - Chemical functions in Dumas method nitrometer apparatus

questiontext.text:
The diagram below depicts the nitrometer assembly used in Dumas method for the quantitative estimation of nitrogen in an organic compound:

In this apparatus, which reagent is used as Solution S, which gaseous component does it absorb, and what is the chemical identity of Gas G collected in the graduated tube?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Principle of Dumas Method
In Dumas method, the organic compound containing nitrogen is completely oxidised by heating with copper(II) oxide (\(\mathrm{CuO}\)) in an atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\): \[ \mathrm{C}_x\mathrm{H}_y\mathrm{N}_z + \left(2x + \frac{y}{2}\right)\mathrm{CuO} \longrightarrow x\mathrm{CO}_2 + \frac{y}{2}\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \frac{z}{2}\mathrm{N}_2 + \left(2x + \frac{y}{2}\right)\mathrm{Cu} \] Any traces of nitrogen oxides formed are reduced back to elemental nitrogen by passing over a heated copper gauze.

Step 2: Role of Solution S in the Nitrometer
The resulting mixture of gases consists of excess \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), water vapour, and dinitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}_2\)). The gaseous mixture is transferred into a nitrometer filled with concentrated potassium hydroxide solution (typically \(40\%\) \(\mathrm{KOH}\)), denoted as Solution S. As the gas bubbles through Solution S, all the \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) is completely absorbed by forming soluble potassium carbonate: \[ 2\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{CO}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{CO}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \]

Step 3: Identity of Gas G
Dinitrogen gas (\(\mathrm{N}_2\)) is chemically unreactive towards aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\) and insoluble in concentrated alkali. Consequently, pure \(\mathrm{N}_2\) gas rises to the top of the graduated nitrometer tube and collects above Solution S as Gas G.

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
Solution S is concentrated aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\) solution which absorbs \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), and Gas G is pure dinitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}_2\)).

answer.text: Solution S is concentrated \(\mathrm{KOH}\) solution, which absorbs \(\mathrm{CO}_2\); Gas G is \(\mathrm{N}_2\)
Solution S is concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), which absorbs \(\mathrm{N}_2\); Gas G is \(\mathrm{CO}_2\)
Solution S is concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution, which absorbs \(\mathrm{N}_2\); Gas G is \(\mathrm{NH}_3\)
Solution S is pyrogallol solution, which absorbs \(\mathrm{O}_2\); Gas G is \(\mathrm{NO}\)
